title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Non-intrusive Model Reduction under Data Scarcity
authors: Vivian Zhang, Tomoki Koike, Atticus Rex, Elizabeth Qian
abstract: Many-query analyses, in which a computational model is repeatedly evaluated, play an important role in uncertainty quantification and optimization for engineering design. However, many-query analyses can be prohibitively expensive when considering high-fidelity numerical models, especially those governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). Surrogate modeling replaces costly simulations with cheap approximations, enabling practical uncertainty quantification and design workflows. Machine learning (ML) approaches to surrogate modeling have gained significant traction in the development of surrogate models due to their non-intrusive nature; they do not require access to the underlying simulation code. The Operator Inference (OpInf) approach, in particular, fits reduced operators to state and corresponding time derivative data. However, high-fidelity training data is scarce due to limited computational budgets, and OpInf models trained on such scarce data often exhibit high variance, a critical liability in high-risk engineering design. We propose Multifidelity Operator Inference (MF-OpInf), which reduces this variance by supplementing scarce high-fidelity snapshots with abundant low-fidelity data drawn from coarser discretizations of the same problem. MF-OpInf handles data across varying fidelity levels by utilizing a multifidelity linear regression framework to estimate the reduced operators. Numerical experiments on model PDE problems demonstrate that MF-OpInf predicts PDE solution fields with higher accuracy compared to the high-fidelity-only OpInf with the same computational budget.

infographic.key_insight: Multifidelity Operator Inference combines scarce high-fidelity data with abundant coarse-model data to reduce variance in learned reduced-order models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate, inexpensive PDE surrogates can support repeated simulations for uncertainty quantification and engineering design under limited training budgets.
method: Learn reduced operators non-intrusively from state snapshots and corresponding time derivatives.
Supplement high-fidelity snapshots with data from coarser discretizations of the same problem.
Estimate reduced operators using multifidelity linear regression.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments on model PDE problems show more accurate solution-field predictions than high-fidelity-only Operator Inference at the same computational budget.
infographic.watch_item: Results are demonstrated on model PDEs; effectiveness for complex engineering systems and different coarse discretizations remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Non-intrusive Model Reduction under Data Scarcity

title: Block-Sparse Gauss-Newton Optimization of Finite Basis Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Sparse Automatic Differentiation Approach
authors: Denis Korolev, Adrian Hill, Jeeeun Lee
abstract: In this work, we develop an efficient Gauss-Newton optimization approach for finite basis physics-informed neural networks (FBPINNs). The key ingredient is the overlapping domain decomposition architecture of FBPINNs, which localizes the influence of each subnetwork and induces block sparsity in both the residual Jacobian and the corresponding Gauss-Newton matrix. We characterize this structure and exploit it through sparse automatic differentiation, using graph coloring to partition structurally orthogonal Jacobian columns or rows. This reduces differentiation costs and memory requirements while preserving all structurally nonzero derivative information. The resulting compressed Jacobian representations allow us to assemble the Gauss-Newton system directly in block-sparse form, enabling the use of sparse direct solvers and preconditioned iterative methods. In this way, the otherwise expensive second-order optimization problem is reduced to scalable sparse linear algebra. We demonstrate the approach on multiscale PDEs, where accurate approximation requires rich neural network parametrizations and large numbers of collocation points. Numerical experiments show that our block-sparse Gauss-Newton method attains high accuracy and substantially accelerates optimization relative to first-order baselines while remaining computationally tractable for large problem sizes.

infographic.key_insight: Overlapping domain decomposition in FBPINNs creates block-sparse derivative structure that makes Gauss–Newton optimization more scalable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Exploiting this sparsity can reduce derivative computation and memory costs when training neural PDE solvers for multiscale engineering problems.
method: Identify block sparsity in the residual Jacobian and Gauss–Newton matrix from localized subnetworks.
Use graph-colored sparse automatic differentiation to compress derivative evaluations while retaining structurally nonzero entries.
Assemble block-sparse Gauss–Newton systems for sparse direct or preconditioned iterative solution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Multiscale PDE experiments report high accuracy and substantially faster optimization than first-order baselines, but the abstract provides no numerical speedups or problem sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Practical scalability depends on subdomain overlap, coloring overhead, and sparse linear-solver performance.
infographic.paper_title: Block-Sparse Gauss-Newton Optimization of Finite Basis Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Sparse Automatic Differentiation Approach

title: Catch It Where It Happens: Real Time Error Correction During LLM Reasoning
authors: Rotem Elimelech, Michael Shalyt, Ido Kaminer
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted with mathematical, scientific and engineering work, yet their mistakes are often confidently written and hard to spot. A single wrong step tends to propagate, making the model waste inference tokens following a false premise. Existing safeguards either check only the final answer and restart from scratch, or rely on a verifier LLM that competes for GPU capacity and slows down response time. We propose online, deterministic verification: many kinds of reasoning steps can be validated by code, so a step can be verified in real time, as it is written, without any model call or GPU use. Whenever a check fails, we point out the mistake and let the model continue from the same spot. We demonstrate this approach on symbolic mathematics, where derivations already contain explicit expressions that a computer algebra system can check in milliseconds. Tested on the ASyMoB benchmark with three open-weights models, our online validation improves accuracy by 1.4-5.6 percentage points, corresponding to a 1.8-14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers, while increasing token usage by only 6-7%. Because the verifier is independent of the model, the approach complements progress in LLMs rather than competing with it: every new model can benefit immediately, and the benefit grows as deterministic checkers extend to more kinds of reasoning steps.

infographic.key_insight: Checking symbolic reasoning steps as they are generated lets LLMs correct errors before they propagate, without restarting or calling a verifier model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CPU-based deterministic checks can improve reliability in checkable mathematical workflows without consuming additional verifier GPU capacity.
method: Validate explicit symbolic expressions online with a computer algebra system.
Flag failed checks immediately and let the LLM continue from the error location.
Use code-based verification rather than a separate verifier LLM.
infographic.evidence_signal: On ASyMoB with three open-weights models, accuracy improved by 1.4–5.6 percentage points, with a 1.8–14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers and 6–7% more tokens.
infographic.watch_item: Results are demonstrated for symbolic mathematics; broader applicability depends on which reasoning steps deterministic checkers can validate.
infographic.paper_title: Catch It Where It Happens: Real Time Error Correction During LLM Reasoning

title: The balance between feature learning and collapse in dynamical systems-based generative models
authors: Julian Brandon, Bruno Loureiro, N Alex Cayco-Gajic, Arthur Pellegrino
abstract: Over the past decade, a growing body of work has established that implicit biases in learning dynamics fundamentally shape the solutions found by neural networks, governing their learned features and generalisation performance. However, despite these strides in deep learning theory, far less is known about representation learning in generative models based on dynamical systems, from normalising flows to diffusion. Importantly, empirical evidence suggests that continuous-time generative models can be prone to mode collapse, yet a learning theory explaining such biases remains elusive. To address this, we use tools from dynamical systems and operator theory to express the gradient flow of a general class of stochastic differential equations as a composition of linear operators, allowing us to relate collapse to low-rank biases in generative models. In variational inference and flow-matching tasks, we show that this bias can manifest in two different mechanisms: i) where collapsed models are stable fixed points of the gradient flow, or ii) in sequential feature learning, where smaller modes take progressively longer to be learned, producing an effective collapse for a fixed training budget. Together these findings point to a trade-off between feature learning and collapse, suggesting an operator view as a step towards a unified framework for understanding the learning dynamics of dynamical systems-based generative models.

infographic.key_insight: Low-rank biases in training dynamics can make dynamical systems-based generative models collapse or learn smaller modes too slowly to capture them within a fixed training budget.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For flow- and diffusion-based generators, missing modes may reflect either stable collapse or slow feature learning, making the distinction important when diagnosing training.
method: Express gradient flow for a general class of stochastic differential equations as compositions of linear operators.
Relate these operators to low-rank biases in generative learning.
Analyze collapse mechanisms in variational inference and flow-matching tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports stable collapsed fixed points and sequential feature learning in variational inference and flow-matching settings, but provides no datasets or quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish how broadly these mechanisms apply to practical architectures or discrete-time training.
infographic.paper_title: The balance between feature learning and collapse in dynamical systems-based generative models

title: Proximal point algorithm for interval valued optimization problems with application to lasso problem
authors: Anurag Jayswal, Sunidhi, Caihong Han
abstract: In this paper, we consider a class of unconstrained interval valued optimization problems and using a suitable scalarization technique, we formulate an associated scalarized optimization problem and establish the relationships between the optimal solution of the scalarized problem and the $LU$-nondominated solution of the considered optimization problem. Based on this framework, we propose a proximal point algorithm and derive the global convergence of the sequence generated by the proposed algorithm along with the sublinear and linear rate of convergence for convex and strongly convex cases, respectively. Finally, we provide suitable numerical experiments along with comparative analysis with an existing method and applicability of the proposed algorithm on an interval valued lasso regression problem, highlighting its potential in machine learning models with uncertain data.

infographic.key_insight: Scalarization connects interval-valued optimization to scalar problems, enabling a proximal point algorithm with global convergence and convexity-dependent rates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a mathematically grounded approach to interval-valued lasso regression for machine learning with uncertain data.
method: Scalarize an unconstrained interval-valued objective and relate scalar optima to LU-nondominated solutions.
Apply a proximal point algorithm to the scalarized problem.
Establish sublinear convergence for convex problems and linear convergence for strongly convex problems.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments, comparison with an existing method, and an interval-valued lasso application, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance depends on scalarization choices and proximal subproblem costs, which are not detailed in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Proximal point algorithm for interval valued optimization problems with application to lasso problem

title: Learning the Brownian Motion in Machine Learning for Parametric Parabolic PDEs: A Backward Quadrature Approach
authors: Qiang Han, Shaolin Ji, Yanan Qi
abstract: We propose a backward quadrature learning (BQL) method for solving high dimensional parametric semilinear parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs). To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to extend the applicability of BSDE-based stochastic numerical methods to this class of PDEs. Specifically, inspired by the approach of learning the random variables (LRV)~\cite{BeckerJentzenMullerWurstemberger2024}, BQL incorporates learnable quadrature for Brownian increments at each time level into the backward recursion of BSDEs, enabling more efficient layerwise approximation of local conditional expectations. Furthermore, BQL introduces a continuation surrogate to facilitate the transfer of value-function information from subsequent to preceding time levels, avoiding nested quadrature while controlling the propagation of local approximation errors. Our main theoretical contribution is the derivation of a global error bound that explicitly characterizes the decomposition of the total error, together with a proof of first-order mean-square convergence under suitable approximation and integrability assumptions. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate that BQL achieves competitive solution accuracy while substantially reducing the amortized computational cost per query. For the HJB benchmark across the tested dimensions, with $Q=7$ parameter queries, BQL achieves computational cost reductions of approximately 40-fold and 4-fold compared with P$^2$INN~[2] and FBSNN~[3], respectively.

infographic.key_insight: Backward quadrature learning (BQL) learns quadrature for Brownian increments within backward BSDE recursion to solve high-dimensional parametric semilinear parabolic PDEs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: BQL can reduce amortized computation when repeatedly evaluating PDE solutions across parameter settings.
method: Learn Brownian-increment quadrature at each time level to approximate local conditional expectations.
Transfer value-function information backward using a continuation surrogate, avoiding nested quadrature.
Derive a global error decomposition and prove first-order mean-square convergence under suitable assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the HJB benchmark across tested dimensions, BQL reports competitive accuracy and approximately 40× and 4× computational cost reductions versus P²INN and FBSNN, respectively, for seven parameter queries.
infographic.watch_item: Convergence depends on approximation and integrability assumptions; reported cost gains should not be generalized beyond the tested query workload and benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: Learning the Brownian Motion in Machine Learning for Parametric Parabolic PDEs: A Backward Quadrature Approach

title: Megrez: A Knowledge-Guided Agent for Formal Mathematics over MK Set Theory
authors: Tiancheng Xu, Wensheng Yu
abstract: General-purpose coding agents equipped with proof-assistant tools have shown strong performance on standalone competition problems, yet cumulative textbook formalization inside a low-resource mathematical library still faces three obstacles: aligning textbook concepts with library declarations, keeping long-horizon search synchronized with live proof states, and integrating locally verified proofs reliably into a growing codebase. We present Megrez, a knowledge-guided formalization agent for Rocq libraries built on Morse--Kelley (MK) set theory. Megrez coordinates a general coding agent through three mechanisms: (1) a source-rebuildable knowledge graph merging formal declarations, compiler references, and curated metadata to support retrieval via Chinese aliases, concept clusters, proof dependencies, and multi-lane full-text ranking; (2) a feedback-driven 1--5 tactic short-burst proving loop paired with a goal-local branch ledger and exponential-interval structured reflection; and (3) a three-check acceptance pipeline (statement fidelity, axiom auditing, and full builds) coupled with a multi-corpus Provider stack and a candidate-bound recoverable batch state machine. Deployment and evaluation on a point-set topology corpus demonstrate effective cross-chapter formalization and scalable premise retrieval.

infographic.key_insight: Megrez coordinates a general coding agent with library knowledge, live proof feedback, and integration checks to formalize textbook mathematics in Rocq over MK set theory.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The design addresses practical bottlenecks in growing formal libraries: finding relevant declarations, tracking proof states, and safely integrating verified results.
method: Rebuildable knowledge graph combines declarations, compiler references, and curated metadata for multilingual, dependency-aware retrieval.
Short bursts of 1–5 tactics use proof-state feedback, a goal-local branch ledger, and structured reflection at exponential intervals.
Statement-fidelity checks, axiom audits, and full builds gate acceptance, supported by multi-corpus providers and recoverable batch execution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Deployment and evaluation on a point-set topology corpus report effective cross-chapter formalization and scalable premise retrieval, without quantitative results in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the evaluated topology corpus remains unclear, and maintaining curated metadata may add implementation overhead.
infographic.paper_title: Megrez: A Knowledge-Guided Agent for Formal Mathematics over MK Set Theory

title: Trust, but verify, audit and attribute: a human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced research results
authors: György Eigner, Patrik P. Süli, Roland Hollós
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems now produce research results in bulk: in October 2026 a single laboratory released more than 700 AI-generated mathematics manuscripts, only part of them with machine-checked proofs. Such volumes will be checked mostly by AI agents that call specialised software. A passing check certifies only the artefact that was checked. For proofs translated into the proof assistant Lean, it has been shown that this artefact may state something other than the author's text, and that deciding whether a translation is faithful is undecidable in general. The human researcher therefore stays in the loop, and human and AI contributions must be recorded. We propose a domain-independent, human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced results. Validated, agent-usable tools with different grounds of trust check the results; a fidelity audit asks whether each check addressed the claim as stated; the human decides at fixed points; and a dialog report attributes the work to the human and to the AI. We describe two automatic implementations of the tool layer, for mathematics (Wolfram Language, MATLAB, Lean) and statistics (Python and R), and run the mathematical one on a two-claim example. An ambiguous claim was split into two readings, one refuted and one proved.

infographic.key_insight: A passing automated check validates only the checked artefact, not necessarily the original research claim, so fidelity audits and human decisions remain essential.
infographic.engineering_relevance: AI-assisted research pipelines should combine validated checking tools, explicit human review gates, and records attributing human and AI contributions.
method: Use validated, agent-usable tools with different grounds of trust to check results.
Audit whether each check addresses the claim as stated, with human decisions at fixed points.
Produce a dialog report attributing work to humans and AI.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper describes mathematics and statistics tool-layer implementations and tests the mathematics implementation on a two-claim example, splitting an ambiguous claim into one refuted reading and one proved reading.
infographic.watch_item: Translation fidelity is undecidable in general, so automated proof checking cannot eliminate the need for human interpretation.
infographic.paper_title: Trust, but verify, audit and attribute: a human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced research results

title: ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification
authors: Martim Afonso, Inês Lynce, Maurizio Morisio, João F. Ferreira
abstract: Formal verification using proof assistants provides strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing proofs remains labor-intensive and requires significant expertise. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating proof synthesis. However, these approaches typically constrain the model to a rigid tactic-generation loop, in which the surrounding system controls premise retrieval, proof-state management, and backtracking. We introduce ProofCoder, an agentic proof-synthesis system for Rocq that approaches theorem proving from a coding-agent perspective. Rather than generating tactics within a fixed loop, ProofCoder reasons continuously throughout proof search and uses proof-assistant feedback to decide when to gather additional information, inspect proof states, revise previously generated proof fragments, or backtrack to an earlier point in the proof. This allows it to iteratively construct, repair, and refine proofs, at either tactic-level or whole-proof granularity. We evaluate ProofCoder on 280 challenging verification tasks from the AutoRocq Benchmark. On the best-performing configurations, ProofCoder increases proof success from 47% to 60% over the state-of-theart AutoRocq system, corresponding to a 27.7% relative improvement at approximately half the cost. Our ablations identify continuous reasoning as a key design choice: without it, the agent solves fewer lemmas at substantially higher cost, backtracks four to six times more often, and more frequently discards its own revisions. Whole-proof and tactic-level generation achieve similar success rates but follow distinct search and repair strategies. These results suggest that effective automated software verification requires more than improved tactic selection: continuous reasoning and feedback-guided proof revision are critical ingredients for robust proof synthesis.

infographic.key_insight: ProofCoder improves automated Rocq proof synthesis by continuously reasoning over proof-assistant feedback rather than following a rigid tactic-generation loop.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Feedback-guided proof construction and repair could reduce the effort and cost of formally verifying software.
method: Treat theorem proving as an agentic coding task.
Use proof-assistant feedback to guide information gathering, proof-state inspection, revision, and backtracking.
Construct and repair proofs at tactic-level or whole-proof granularity.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 280 AutoRocq Benchmark tasks, the best configurations increased proof success from 47% to 60% versus AutoRocq—a 27.7% relative improvement—at approximately half the cost.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to the reported Rocq benchmark; generalization to other proof assistants and verification workloads remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification

title: Discrete Model-Based Diffusion for Combinatorial Optimization in Multi-Robot Task Allocation
authors: Haejoon Lee, Thomas Marshall Vielmetti, Xinyi Wang, Dimitra Panagou
abstract: Decision making in multi-agent and multi-robot systems often involves discrete decision variables, leading to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems that must be solved within seconds for near real-time implementation. Denoising diffusion has emerged as a powerful tool for such problems, but existing approaches face a trade-off: Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) incorporates diffusion in sampling-based optimization (SBO) without training but only over continuous spaces, while existing diffusion-based combinatorial solvers operate over discrete spaces but require offline training. To this end, we propose Discrete Model-Based Diffusion (Discrete MBD), a training-free SBO method that directly optimizes discrete variables by approximating categorical reverse transition distributions through Monte Carlo sampling. We establish a finite-step lower bound on the probability of finding a global minimizer and show that this bound converges to one as the number of denoising steps increases. Extensive experiments on generic integer programs and heterogeneous multi-robot coalition formation and scheduling demonstrate that Discrete MBD outperforms SBO baselines in nearly all settings while achieving solution quality competitive with that of mixed-integer programming and reinforcement learning methods at a fraction of their computational cost.

infographic.key_insight: Discrete Model-Based Diffusion performs training-free combinatorial optimization directly over discrete variables using diffusion-guided sampling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets fast multi-robot coalition formation and scheduling, with reported solution quality competitive with mixed-integer programming and reinforcement learning at lower computational cost.
method: Use denoising diffusion within sampling-based optimization over discrete variables.
Approximate categorical reverse transitions with Monte Carlo sampling.
Establish a finite-step lower bound on global-optimum discovery probability that approaches one as denoising steps increase.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on generic integer programs and heterogeneous multi-robot allocation problems outperform sampling-based optimization baselines in nearly all tested settings.
infographic.watch_item: The asymptotic probability guarantee does not establish a practical runtime guarantee; Monte Carlo sampling and denoising budgets remain implementation concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Discrete Model-Based Diffusion for Combinatorial Optimization in Multi-Robot Task Allocation

title: BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
authors: Rui Zou, Xin Zhao, Mengqi Wei, Ji-Rong Wen
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning but still produce incorrect solutions to complex problems, indicating the need for more reliable self-correction mechanisms. Mathematical self-correction typically identifies errors through verification, which can proceed backward or forward. The two directions provide complementary verification capabilities. Backward verification checks a candidate answer against the original constraints, bypassing complex intermediate reasoning, but cannot ensure correct reasoning or objective completeness. Forward verification follows the problem conditions and current solution, enabling it to locate reasoning errors and assess objective completeness, but may overlook key constraints in complex solution chains. We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification. BiVerify begins with backward verification to screen the answer against the original constraints, followed by forward verification of the reasoning process; subsequent direction switching, state resetting, and re-verification are governed by verification outcomes. Upon failure, the system revises the candidate or verification flow until the same candidate passes both directions. We also introduce shared mathematical tools that separate logical reasoning from precise computation. We systematically evaluate BiVerify on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks using multiple mainstream DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models. BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline evaluated in this work by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 percentage points on GPT. Further analysis shows that BiVerify's overall performance exceeds that of either verification direction alone.

infographic.key_insight: BiVerify improves mathematical self-correction by requiring the same candidate solution to pass both backward constraint checks and forward reasoning checks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Bidirectional verification offers a structured way to improve LLM math reliability by combining complementary checks with shared tools for precise computation.
method: Start with backward verification against the original problem constraints, then verify reasoning and objective completeness forward.
Dynamically switch direction, reset verification state, and revise candidates or verification flow when checks fail.
Use shared mathematical tools to separate logical reasoning from precise computation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five challenging math benchmarks and multiple DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models, BiVerify exceeds the strongest evaluated representative public baseline by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with a 31.2-point margin on GPT.
infographic.watch_item: Repeated verification and revision may increase latency and computation cost; the abstract does not quantify this overhead or guarantee correctness.
infographic.paper_title: BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction

title: Orthogonal Updates for the Win: Towards Accelerated Adaptive Minimax Optimization
authors: Zhiwei Zhai, Xinyu Wang, Wenjing Yan, Lei Ding, Ying-Jun Angela Zhang
abstract: Single-loop minimax methods are appealing for modern machine learning, but standard stochastic gradient updates can be unstable and oscillatory under tightly coupled primal-dual dynamics, making performance notoriously sensitive to stepsizes. To fundamentally improve stability, we develop an orthogonal update framework tailored to minimax optimization, which applies updates along orthogonalized directions to reduce update anisotropy. However, orthogonalization reshapes the optimization geometry and makes coordinating primal-dual stepsizes even more delicate. To overcome this challenge, we develop AdaSGDA, which equips orthogonal updates with an adaptive stepsize rule driven by accumulated gradient norms. This mechanism automatically balances coupled primal-dual progress under orthogonalization, yielding an effectively parameter-free method for nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization. We prove that AdaSGDA avoids problem-dependent tuning while attaining the state-of-the-art $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/4}\right)$ convergence rate. We further propose AdaSGDA-VR, which incorporates a carefully designed variance reduction scheme and achieves the faster $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/3}\right)$ rate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our methods deliver competitive performance compared to existing minimax optimization methods.

infographic.key_insight: Orthogonalized updates paired with gradient-norm-based adaptive stepsizes stabilize coupled minimax optimization while avoiding problem-dependent tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce stepsize-tuning effort in machine-learning systems trained through coupled minimization and maximization.
method: Orthogonalize update directions to reduce update anisotropy.
Use accumulated gradient norms to adapt and balance primal-dual stepsizes in AdaSGDA.
Add variance reduction in AdaSGDA-VR to improve the theoretical convergence rate.
infographic.evidence_signal: For nonconvex–strongly-concave problems, the paper proves convergence rates of O(T^(-1/4)) for AdaSGDA and O(T^(-1/3)) for AdaSGDA-VR; the abstract reports competitive experimental performance without specifying benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The stated guarantees rely on strong concavity in the maximization variable and do not establish performance for general nonconvex–nonconcave problems.
infographic.paper_title: Orthogonal Updates for the Win: Towards Accelerated Adaptive Minimax Optimization

title: LLM-Assisted Advances in the Ropelength Problem
authors: Alexander Klotz
abstract: This work summarizes some updates to the ropelength problem, concerning the shortest possible contour length of a unit-thickness knot, that were derived with the assistance of ChatGPT-5.6 Luna. The first of two main results is that the universal lower bound for a knot with crossing number C has been improved from $L\geq1.105C^{3/4}$ to $L\geq2.0996C^{3/4}$, achieved by further separating local and global terms in an optimization integral. The second main result is a bound relating ropelength to stick number (s), such that $L\geqπ(s-1)$. This implies stronger lower bounds for the ropelengths of at least 41 torus knots, and a specific class of pretzel knots. Other results include an improved packing-based lower bound for T(Q,Q) links and an optimized standard parameterization for torus knots. There were many problems for which the LLM was unable to render assistance, for example in reducing the numerical coefficients or scalings of known universal upper bounds.

infographic.key_insight: The paper reports sharper knot-ropelength lower bounds: L ≥ 2.0996C^(3/4) for crossing number C and L ≥ π(s−1) for stick number s.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These bounds provide theoretical benchmarks for optimizing knotted filaments and assessing geometric packing constraints.
method: Use LLM assistance to develop mathematical bounds.
Separate local and global terms in an optimization integral.
Relate ropelength to stick number and optimize a standard torus-knot parameterization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improving the universal coefficient from 1.105 to 2.0996 and obtaining stronger lower bounds for at least 41 torus knots and a specific pretzel-knot class.
infographic.watch_item: LLM assistance did not yield improvements to the coefficients or scaling of known universal upper bounds.
infographic.paper_title: LLM-Assisted Advances in the Ropelength Problem

title: Geometry-Dependent Approximation and Stability Properties of Shallow ReLU$^k$ Networks on Bounded Euclidean Domains
authors: Yuqing Liu, Tong Mao, Jinchao Xu
abstract: On bounded Euclidean domains, we study how hidden-parameter geometry affects shallow ReLU$^k$ networks through results on approximation rates, saturation-type lower bounds, Gram and stiffness matrix spectra, Bernstein and Marcinkiewicz--Zygmund inequalities, discrete least-squares recovery, and inverse approximation. Our analysis uses smooth localization and dyadic Fourier estimates. We quantify parameter geometry by the fill distance $h$ and antipodal separation distance $\underline h$. For the prescribed network space $L_n^k$, representative approximation estimates take the form \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \inf_{g_n\in L_n^k}\|f-g_n\|_{\mathcal L^2(Ω')}&\lesssim h^r\|f\|_{\mathcal H^r(Ω)},\\ \inf_{g_n\in L_n^k}\|f-g_n\|_{\mathcal L^2(Ω)}&\gtrsim \underline h^{\frac{d+2k+1}{2}}\|f\|_{\mathcal L^2(Ω')}. \end{aligned} \end{equation*} The upper bound exploits target regularity up to the critical order $\frac{d+2k+1}{2}$, while the lower bound applies asymptotically to fixed targets smoother than this order. The upper estimate holds on an interior subdomain $Ω'$, whereas the lower estimate concerns the larger domain $Ω$. We also obtain geometry-dependent spectral estimates that quantify conditioning and coefficient stability. Further results establish norm discretization and regularized recovery from function values, and infer target regularity from approximation rates under coefficient or separation conditions. Altogether, these results describe how parameter geometry governs approximation accuracy, the stability of coefficient representations, discrete recovery, and the regularity information contained in convergence rates.

infographic.key_insight: Hidden-parameter coverage and separation govern the approximation accuracy, conditioning, and recovery stability of shallow ReLU^k networks on bounded domains.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide theoretical guidance for choosing hidden parameters and assessing coefficient stability in least-squares network fitting.
method: Measure parameter geometry using fill distance h and antipodal separation distance h̲.
Use smooth localization and dyadic Fourier estimates to derive approximation bounds and spectral estimates.
Establish norm discretization, regularized recovery, and inverse approximation results.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical bounds rather than empirical benchmarks, with approximation gains up to regularity (d+2k+1)/2 and saturation-type lower bounds for fixed smoother targets.
infographic.watch_item: The upper approximation bound holds on an interior subdomain, while the lower bound concerns the larger domain; they are not directly matching error estimates.
infographic.paper_title: Geometry-Dependent Approximation and Stability Properties of Shallow ReLU$^k$ Networks on Bounded Euclidean Domains

title: Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models
authors: Yibo Miao, Yichuan Cao, Xiao-Shan Gao, Yinpeng Dong
abstract: LLMs are powerful but incur substantial inference cost, which can be exploited by malicious users to induce overly long outputs, increasing latency and operational expense. Prior resource consumption attacks either coerce repetition or suppress the end-of-sequence token by lowering its logit value. However, with autoregressive, sampling-based generation, the search space grows exponentially with length and small deviations or unstable trajectories can derail optimization, limiting attack effectiveness and stability. To address this issue, we introduce Chatter Attack, a novel class of resource consumption attacks that optimize adversarial prompts to induce predefined short target phrases, thereby avoiding search-space explosion while still eliciting long responses. Specifically, Chatter Attack triggers self-doubt using short doubt-inducing phrases as the target, and sustains this state throughout generation via inference attention loss and global entropy loss. To extend to black-box settings, we further propose a novel Bayesian Prompt Optimization (BPO) method, which models the objective function globally by constructing a discrete token kernel, efficiently exploring the entire search space using prior information. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets show that our method outperforms baselines, with maximum response length increases to 31.5$\times$, and revealing practical resource-depletion risks for real-world LLM inference services.

infographic.key_insight: Chatter Attack induces short, doubt-triggering phrases that can steer LLMs into prolonged responses, amplifying inference resource consumption.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The attack highlights availability and cost risks for LLM services, motivating output-token limits, generation timeouts, and resource monitoring.
method: Optimize adversarial prompts toward short doubt-inducing target phrases rather than entire long responses.
Use inference attention loss and global entropy loss to sustain self-doubt during generation.
Extend to black-box settings with Bayesian Prompt Optimization using a discrete token kernel.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experiments across multiple models and datasets, outperforming baselines with response-length increases of up to 31.5×.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify black-box query costs or whether effectiveness persists under strict output-token and time limits.
infographic.paper_title: Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models

title: Total variation error bounds for Schrödinger-Föllmer samplers
authors: Xiaojie Wang, Xiaoyan Zhang
abstract: Sampling from high-dimensional, multimodal target distributions plays a fundamental role in scientific computing, statistics and machine learning. Recently, the Schrödinger-Föllmer sampler (SFS) has been proposed by Huang et al. (IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory, 2025) as an efficient sampling algorithm that transports the degenerate distribution at $t=0$ to the target distribution at $t=1$, without relying on long-time ergodicity. In this paper, we establish non-asymptotic error bounds for SFS in the total variation distance by deriving regularization estimates for the associated Kolmogorov equation via the Bismut-Elworthy-Li formula. When the drift can be computed exactly, a convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}( h|\ln h|)$ was obtained under certain smoothness conditions on the drift with a uniform time step-size $h>0$. When the drift is approximated by Monte Carlo methods, we obtain a convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}( h|\ln h|+ 1/M)$, where $M$ is the number of samples used in the Monte Carlo approximation. This yields a sharper dependence on $M$ than the existing bound $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{M})$ in the $L^2$-Wasserstein distance in the aforementioned paper, by turning the total variation error to the weak error analysis in the setting of non-smooth test functions. Numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the convergence rate with respect to the time step-size $h$ and the Monte Carlo sample size $M$ and the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

infographic.key_insight: The paper establishes non-asymptotic total variation error bounds for Schrödinger–Föllmer samplers: O(h|ln h|) with exact drift and O(h|ln h| + 1/M) with Monte Carlo drift.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These bounds guide time-step and Monte Carlo sample-budget choices for high-dimensional, multimodal sampling without relying on long-time ergodicity.
method: Derive Kolmogorov equation regularization estimates using the Bismut–Elworthy–Li formula.
Analyze total variation error through weak error estimates for non-smooth test functions.
Bound errors from time discretization and Monte Carlo drift approximation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments illustrate convergence with respect to time-step size h and Monte Carlo sample size M, alongside sampler effectiveness.
infographic.watch_item: The rates require drift regularity assumptions; the improved 1/M dependence is compared with an earlier 1/√M bound in a different metric, L²-Wasserstein distance.
infographic.paper_title: Total variation error bounds for Schrödinger-Föllmer samplers

title: On the Global Convergence of Stochastic Adam for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
authors: Yihang Gao
abstract: The Adam optimizer is widely used to train neural networks with highly nonlinear and nonconvex objective functions. Remarkably, Adam often drives the empirical training loss nearly to zero. This phenomenon has been partially explained by neural tangent kernel (NTK) analyses of gradient descent (GD) and stochastic gradient descent (SGD). However, analyzing Adam presents additional challenges. Its first-moment momentum couples stochastic gradients across iterations, while its adaptive second-moment preconditioner depends on the same stochastic gradient used in the update. In this paper, we establish linear convergence guarantees for Adam in training sufficiently wide two-layer neural networks with either full-batch or minibatch gradients. For full-batch Adam, we construct a Lyapunov function to control the effect of historical momentum. For minibatch Adam, our analysis builds on an exact virtual-iterate representation, a conditional analysis of the dependence between stochastic gradients and adaptive preconditioners, and uniform concentration bounds for the second-moment estimates. We prove geometric decay of the empirical loss for full-batch Adam and geometric decay in restricted expectation on a high-probability event for minibatch Adam. Beyond regression, we extend our convergence analysis to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for solving the Poisson equation, where differential operators and separate sampling of interior and boundary points introduce additional challenges. We establish analogous global convergence guarantees for both deterministic and stochastic Adam under explicit conditions on network width and Adam's parameters, characterizing the effects of minibatch size on convergence. These results help bridge the gap between Adam's empirical success and its theoretical understanding, providing sharper convergence guarantees for PINNs than existing analyses.

infographic.key_insight: Adam achieves provable geometric loss decay for sufficiently wide two-layer networks, including Poisson-equation PINNs, under explicit parameter conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide theoretical guidance on network width, Adam parameters, and minibatch-size effects when training PINN solvers.
method: Construct a Lyapunov function to control momentum in full-batch Adam.
Analyze minibatch Adam using exact virtual iterates, conditional dependence analysis, and second-moment concentration bounds.
Extend the guarantees to Poisson PINNs with separately sampled interior and boundary points.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence guarantees, not numerical benchmarks; minibatch loss decay holds in restricted expectation on a high-probability event.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees require sufficiently wide two-layer networks and explicit Adam parameter conditions, so they do not automatically extend to practical deep PINNs.
infographic.paper_title: On the Global Convergence of Stochastic Adam for Physics-Informed Neural Networks

title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models
authors: Zijian Zhang, Rizhen Hu, Jiangweizhi Peng, Shiyang Li, Sujay Bhatt, Sihan Zeng
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.

infographic.key_insight: AutoScaffold turns reinforcement-learning experience into adaptive training guidance that improves language-model performance even after the guidance is removed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A frozen teacher automates training-support design across reasoning and engineering tasks, reducing reliance on manually crafted, domain-specific scaffolds.
method: Periodically inspect student training experience to diagnose learning bottlenecks.
Generate shared task-class strategies and hints for individual hard tasks.
Adapt support as the student improves, then remove all scaffolds at evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four domains, scaffold-free evaluation outperformed corresponding RL baselines; in math, the student surpassed QuestA’s reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps.
infographic.watch_item: Fewer student training steps do not establish lower total compute cost; teacher inference and scaffold-generation overhead also need accounting.
infographic.paper_title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models

title: A Stability Analysis of AdamW: Unstable Equilibria and Non-Convergence
authors: Baiyu Su, Lizhang Chen, Qiang Liu
abstract: AdamW is ubiquitous in deep learning, yet its behavior remains poorly understood. We analyze its dynamics through the lens of dynamical systems and show that AdamW admits an implicit fixed-point objective: its fixed points coincide with the stationary points of a constrained and regularized optimization problem. However, not all of these fixed points are stable under AdamW's dynamics, and stability depends sensitively on curvature, weight decay, and momentum parameters. Even in one-dimensional settings, equilibria may be unstable, and trajectories can exhibit persistent oscillations rather than convergence to them. We further extend the analysis to higher dimensions, deriving sufficient conditions for local stability of the continuous-time dynamics, and propose a convergent modification that preserves AdamW's fixed points. These results clarify what optimization problem AdamW is associated with, when its convergence can be expected, and how its dynamics could inspire more reliable optimizers.

infographic.key_insight: AdamW’s fixed points match stationary points of a constrained, regularized objective, but its dynamics can destabilize them and produce persistent oscillations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The analysis links AdamW’s convergence behavior to curvature, weight decay, and momentum, informing optimizer design and hyperparameter choices.
method: Characterize AdamW’s implicit fixed-point objective.
Analyze equilibrium stability in one and higher dimensions.
Propose a convergent modification preserving AdamW’s fixed points.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical instability results even in one dimension and sufficient local stability conditions for higher-dimensional continuous-time dynamics, but no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Continuous-time local stability conditions should not be assumed to guarantee convergence of discrete-time AdamW in practical training.
infographic.paper_title: A Stability Analysis of AdamW: Unstable Equilibria and Non-Convergence

title: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions
authors: Guneykan Ozgul, Dylan Herman, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Shree Hari Sureshbabu, Shouvanik Chakrabarti
abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a workhorse algorithm for continuous optimization. It is a folk belief among deep learning practitioners that learning rate decay in SGD substantially improves performance. However, it has remained unclear whether learning rate decay offers an asymptotic advantage for global nonconvex optimization. We answer this question in the affirmative by demonstrating a natural class of nonconvex functions for which, we prove that SGD with learning rate decay requires exponentially fewer gradient queries for global optimization than SGD with any fixed learning rate in the small-step size regime. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exponential advantage that has been demonstrated for learning rate decay. The class of functions we consider includes many popular benchmark nonconvex functions. Our results provide a robust explanatory theory for the empirically observed benefits of learning rate decay for global optimization. We show that annealing performs the non-logconcave sampling task associated to the optimization problem in polynomial time, via a novel application of weak Poincaré inequalities.

infographic.key_insight: For a natural class of nonconvex functions, SGD with learning rate decay provably needs exponentially fewer gradient queries for global optimization than any fixed learning rate in the small-step-size regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result gives theoretical support for learning rate decay when seeking global optima on qualifying nonconvex objectives.
method: Analyze a nonconvex function class that includes many popular benchmark functions.
Compare gradient-query complexity for decaying versus fixed learning rates.
Use weak Poincaré inequalities to prove polynomial-time annealing for the associated non-logconcave sampling task.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical complexity guarantees, but no numerical experiments or empirical performance measurements.
infographic.watch_item: The exponential advantage is established for a specific function class and small-step-size fixed-rate comparisons, not arbitrary nonconvex problems or practical training schedules.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions
